title: Πρίαμος ἐξορμᾶται
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hecuba cries out that Priam has lost his wits: no man could face Achilles, who killed so many of their sons and will show no pity, and she wishes she could eat his liver. Priam will not be held back; a god has told him, and if he is to die by the Achaean ships, he accepts it, so long as he first holds his son. He opens the chests and takes out robes, cloaks, carpets, gold, tripods, cauldrons and the Thracian cup. He drives the Trojans from his portico, rebukes them, and then shouts at his nine remaining sons, calling them base shames, while he laments the sons he has lost. The sons ready the mule-wagon and load the ransom. Hecuba brings wine for a libation and bids him pray to Zeus for a bird on the right; Priam agrees at once.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, κώκυσεν δὲ γυνὴ καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, kōkysen de gynē kai ameibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the woman cried out, and answered with a word:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his wife cried out and answered him:
sentences.n: Priam’s speech in the last part closed at 24.199, so this line is the poet’s own narration. Hecuba is not named until 24.283; here she is only γυνή, ‘woman’, a word that in Greek also means ‘wife’. κώκυσεν is the aorist of κωκύω ‘cry out’, a loud, high cry. ἀμείβετο is the middle imperfect ‘answered’, and μύθῳ is a dative, ‘with a word’.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι πῇ δή τοι φρένες οἴχονθ’, ᾗς τὸ πάρος περ
ἔκλε’ ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους ξείνους ἠδ’ οἷσιν ἀνάσσεις;
sentences.tr:
ō moi pēi dē toi phrenes oichonth’, hēis to paros per
ekle’ ep’ anthrōpous xeinous ēd’ hoisin anasseis;
sentences.l:
“Oh me, where indeed are your wits gone, for which formerly
you were famed among stranger men and those you are lord over?
sentences.i: “Oh me, where have your wits gone, the wits for which you were famed before among strangers and among those you rule?
sentences.n: Hecuba begins with a cry, ὤ μοι ‘oh me’, and asks where Priam’s good sense has gone. οἴχονθ’ is οἴχονται, ‘are gone’ (the elided ending could also be οἴχοντο, ‘went’), and ᾗς (= ᾗσι) is the relative ‘for which’, agreeing with φρένες. ἔκλε’ is read as an elided ἔκλεο, ‘you were famed’, from the verb behind κλέος ‘fame’. ξείνους is the epic form of ξένους, ‘strangers’ (foreign men), and οἷσιν ἀνάσσεις is ‘those over whom you are lord’.

sentences.t:
πῶς ἐθέλεις ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν ἐλθέμεν οἶος
ἀνδρὸς ἐς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὅς τοι πολέας τε καὶ ἐσθλοὺς
υἱέας ἐξενάριξε· σιδήρειόν νύ τοι ἦτορ.
sentences.tr:
pōs etheleis epi nēas Achaiōn elthemen oios
andros es ophthalmous hos toi poleas te kai esthlous
huieas exenarixe· sidēreion ny toi ētor.
sentences.l:
How do you wish to the ships of the Achaeans to go, alone,
into the eyes of a man who many, and good,
sons of yours has despoiled? Iron, then, is your heart.
sentences.i: How can you bring yourself to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans, before the eyes of a man who has killed and stripped so many of your good sons? Your heart is iron.
sentences.n: ἐθέλεις is ‘you wish, you are willing’, and ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive ‘to go’, a short form of ἐλθέμεναι; οἶος is ‘alone’. ὅς τοι is ‘who … of yours’, with τοι for σοι. ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω, ‘kill and strip of armour’, built on ἐνάρα ‘spoils’. σιδήρειον is ‘of iron’: she means a heart that feels nothing, but the Greek simply says ‘iron’.

sentences.t:
εἰ γάρ σ’ αἱρήσει καὶ ἐσόψεται ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
ὠμηστὴς καὶ ἄπιστος ἀνὴρ ὅ γε οὔ σ’ ἐλεήσει,
οὐδέ τί σ’ αἰδέσεται.
sentences.tr:
ei gar s’ hairēsei kai esopsetai ophthalmoisin
ōmēstēs kai apistos anēr ho ge ou s’ eleēsei,
oude ti s’ aidesetai.
sentences.l:
For if he takes you and sees you with his eyes,
a raw-feeding and faithless man, that one will not pity you,
nor will he at all respect you.
sentences.i: For if he takes you and sees you with his own eyes, a man who feeds on raw flesh and is faithless, he will not pity you, nor show you any respect.
sentences.n: The man is Achilles, though she does not name him. The futures αἱρήσει and ἐσόψεται, ‘will take’ and ‘will look on’, put the danger as a thing to be expected, not just feared. ὠμηστής is ‘one who eats raw’, a hard word for a man, and ἄπιστος is ‘faithless’, someone who cannot be trusted. ὅ γε is ‘that one’. αἰδέσεται is the future of αἰδέομαι, ‘feel respect for’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ κλαίωμεν ἄνευθεν
ἥμενοι ἐν μεγάρῳ·
sentences.tr:
nyn de klaiōmen aneuthen
hēmenoi en megarōi·
sentences.l:
But now let us weep, apart,
sitting in the hall:
sentences.i: But now, sitting apart in the hall, let us weep:
sentences.n: κλαίωμεν is a present subjunctive used as a call to action, ‘let us weep’. ἄνευθεν means ‘apart, at a distance’; the Greek does not say from whom or from where, and here it fits keeping away from Achilles. ἥμενοι is the participle ‘sitting’ and μεγάρῳ is the hall, the main room of the house. The colon after it opens her reason for giving up hope.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ὥς ποθι Μοῖρα κραταιὴ
γιγνομένῳ ἐπένησε λίνῳ, ὅτε μιν τέκον αὐτή,
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ hōs pothi Moira krataiē
gignomenōi epenēse linōi, hote min tekon autē,
sentences.l:
And for him thus, I suppose, strong Portion
as he was born spun with her thread, when I myself bore him,
sentences.i: For so, I suppose, strong Fate spun for him with her thread when he was born, when I myself bore him,
sentences.n: The δέ in τῷ δ’ gives her reason, much as γάρ would. Μοῖρα is Fate as a person, the power who spins a life; κραταιή is ‘strong’. τῷ is ‘for him’ (Hector), with γιγνομένῳ ‘as he was being born’. ποθι is ‘somewhere, I suppose’, which makes this a guess, not a statement of fact. ἐπένησε is the aorist of ἐπινέω ‘spin to’, and λίνῳ ‘with thread’ is a flax thread. The sentence goes on in the next unit with infinitives. αὐτή is ‘I myself’.

sentences.t:
ἀργίποδας κύνας ἆσαι ἑῶν ἀπάνευθε τοκήων
ἀνδρὶ πάρα κρατερῷ, τοῦ ἐγὼ μέσον ἧπαρ ἔχοιμι
ἐσθέμεναι προσφῦσα·
sentences.tr:
argipodas kynas asai heōn apaneuthe tokēōn
andri para kraterōi, tou egō meson hēpar echoimi
esthemenai prosphysa·
sentences.l:
quick-footed dogs to glut, apart from his own parents,
beside a strong man, whose liver, the middle of it, may I be able
to eat, having fastened on him:
sentences.i: to glut quick-footed dogs, away from his own parents, beside a strong man; may I be able to fasten on him and eat the middle of his liver:
sentences.n: ἆσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to glut’, and the dogs eat his body far from his own people. ἀργίποδας is ‘quick-footed’ (or possibly ‘white-footed’): its first part is the same ἀργ- as in κύνας ἀργούς ‘swift dogs’, whose sense is disputed. μέσον ἧπαρ is ‘the liver, its middle’. ἔχοιμι with ἐσθέμεναι ‘to eat’ is an optative wish, ‘may I be able to’. προσφῦσα is ‘having fastened on’, said by a woman.

sentences.t:
τότ’ ἄντιτα ἔργα γένοιτο
παιδὸς ἐμοῦ, ἐπεὶ οὔ ἑ κακιζόμενόν γε κατέκτα,
sentences.tr:
tot’ antita erga genoito
paidos emou, epei ou he kakizomenon ge katekta,
sentences.l:
then deeds of requital would come to be
for my child, since not acting basely did he kill him,
sentences.i: then there would be deeds of requital for my son, since that man did not kill him while he played the coward,
sentences.n: ἄντιτα is the neuter plural of an adjective meaning ‘in requital, paying back’, and ἔργα ‘deeds’ goes with it. γένοιτο is an optative, ‘would come to be’. παιδός is ‘child’ (here Hector). κακιζόμενον is ‘playing the base man’, that is, acting as a coward; ἑ is ‘him’, and the Greek leaves the killer unnamed. κατέκτα is the aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’. The thought is that Hector died fighting, so only a like death would repay it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πρὸ Τρώων καὶ Τρωϊάδων βαθυκόλπων
ἑσταότ’ οὔτε φόβου μεμνημένον οὔτ’ ἀλεωρῆς.
sentences.tr:
alla pro Trōōn kai Trōïadōn bathykolpōn
hestaot’ oute phobou memnēmenon out’ aleōrēs.
sentences.l:
but in front of the Trojans and the Trojan women, deep-bosomed,
standing, mindful of neither flight nor defence.”
sentences.i: but standing before the Trojans and the deep-bosomed Trojan women, with no thought of flight or of defence.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Hecuba’s speech. ἑσταότ’ and μεμνημένον are both accusative singulars agreeing with ἑ, ‘him’, in the line before: Hector standing and not thinking of escape. φόβου is ‘flight’, the fear that makes men run, and ἀλεωρῆς is ‘defence’, a way of keeping the blow off. βαθυκόλπων ‘deep-bosomed’ describes the Trojan women by the deep fold of their dress.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe gerōn Priamos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: Then Priam, the old man, godlike in form, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: This is the poet’s narration, opening Priam’s answer. αὖτε is ‘in turn, then’, and προσέειπε is ‘addressed’. τὴν is the feminine ‘her’, Hecuba. γέρων is ‘old man’. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’, made from θεός ‘god’ and εἶδος ‘form’; it is Priam’s stock epithet here and describes his looks, not his rank.

sentences.t:
μή μ’ ἐθέλοντ’ ἰέναι κατερύκανε, μὴ δέ μοι αὐτὴ
ὄρνις ἐνὶ μεγάροισι κακὸς πέλευ· οὐδέ με πείσεις.
sentences.tr:
mē m’ ethelont’ ienai katerykane, mē de moi autē
ornis eni megaroisi kakos peleu· oude me peiseis.
sentences.l:
“Do not hold me back as I wish to go, and do not, you yourself,
be an evil bird for me in the halls; you will not persuade me.
sentences.i: “Do not hold me back when I wish to go, and do not yourself be an evil bird for me in the halls: you will not persuade me.
sentences.n: Priam forbids two things with μή and the present imperative: κατερύκανε is a lengthened epic form of the imperative of κατερύκω ‘hold back’, and πέλευ is ‘be’, the imperative of πέλομαι. ἐθέλοντα is ‘wishing’, agreeing with μ’. ὄρνις κακός, ‘an evil bird’, is a bird seen as an omen: her words would be a bad sign for the journey. οὐδέ με πείσεις is the future ‘you will not persuade me’.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν γάρ τίς μ’ ἄλλος ἐπιχθονίων ἐκέλευεν,
ἢ οἳ μάντιές εἰσι θυοσκόοι ἢ ἱερῆες,
ψεῦδός κεν φαῖμεν καὶ νοσφιζοίμεθα μᾶλλον·
sentences.tr:
ei men gar tis m’ allos epichthoniōn ekeleuen,
ē hoi manties eisi thyoskooi ē hierēes,
pseudos ken phaimen kai nosphizoimetha mallon·
sentences.i: For if some other of those who live on earth had ordered me, or one of those who are seers, sacrificing priests, or priests, we should call it a falsehood and all the more turn away from it;
sentences.n: The last line here, 24.222, is word for word 2.81, where Nestor speaks of Agamemnon’s dream, and its English is kept. ἐπιχθονίων is ‘of those upon the earth’, mortals as against gods. μάντις is ‘seer’; θυοσκόος is a rare word for a priest who attends the offerings, whose exact function is not certain; ἱερεύς is ‘priest’. The optatives φαῖμεν and νοσφιζοίμεθα follow the past condition: ‘we should call … and turn away’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἄκουσα θεοῦ καὶ ἐσέδρακον ἄντην,
εἶμι καὶ οὐχ ἅλιον ἔπος ἔσσεται.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’, autos gar akousa theou kai esedrakon antēn,
eimi kai ouch halion epos essetai.
sentences.l:
But now, for I myself heard a god and gazed on him, right in front,
I shall go, and the word will not be in vain.
sentences.i: But now, since I myself heard a god and looked upon him right in front of me, I shall go, and the word will not prove vain.
sentences.n: The contrast is with the human advisers just dismissed: Priam’s authority is a god he has seen and heard. ἄκουσα is the aorist ἤκουσα without its augment, with a genitive of the person heard; ἐσέδρακον is the aorist of εἰσδέρκομαι ‘look at’, with ἐσ- for εἰσ-. θεοῦ is grammatically masculine, but θεός also names a goddess, and the god he means is Iris (24.169–187). ἅλιον is ‘vain’, and ἔσσεται is the epic ἔσται, ‘will be’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ μοι αἶσα
τεθνάμεναι παρὰ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
βούλομαι·
sentences.tr:
ei de moi aisa
tethnamenai para nēusin Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn
boulomai·
sentences.l:
But if my lot is
to die beside the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
I want it:
sentences.i: But if it is my lot to die beside the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans, I want it:
sentences.n: εἰ δέ μοι αἶσα lacks a verb: ‘if to me (it is) a lot’, with τεθνάμεναι ‘to die’ as the thing that is allotted. αἶσα is ‘lot’. βούλομαι ‘I want’ is the main verb of the sentence, and here means that he accepts such a death, and the colon after it promises the reason. χαλκοχιτώνων is ‘bronze-shirted’, the Iliad’s and Odyssey’s epithet for the Achaeans, formed on χαλκός ‘bronze’ and χιτών ‘shirt’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα γάρ με κατακτείνειεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἀγκὰς ἑλόντ’ ἐμὸν υἱόν, ἐπὴν γόου ἐξ ἔρον εἵην.
sentences.tr:
autika gar me katakteineien Achilleus
ankas helont’ emon huion, epēn goou ex eron heiēn.
sentences.l:
for at once may Achilles kill me,
having taken my son in my arms, when I have put away desire of lament.”
sentences.i: for let Achilles kill me at once, when I have taken my son in my arms and had my fill of lament.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Priam’s speech. κατακτείνειεν is an optative of wish, ‘may he kill’. ἑλόντ’ is an accusative singular masculine participle, ‘having taken’, agreeing with με ‘me’, so Priam is the one who holds his son. ἀγκάς is ‘in the arms’. γόου ἐξ ἔρον εἵην is hard: it is read as the split compound ἐξ … εἵην, aorist optative of ἐξίημι ‘send out, put away’, with ἔρον ‘desire’ as its object, so ‘put away the desire for lament’, that is, have had enough of mourning.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ φωριαμῶν ἐπιθήματα κάλ’ ἀνέῳγεν·
sentences.tr: ē kai phōriamōn epithēmata kal’ aneōigen·
sentences.l: He spoke, and the fine lids of the chests he opened:
sentences.i: So he said, and he opened the fine lids of the chests:
sentences.n: ἦ καί is the old ‘he said, and’ that ends a speech and starts the action; the speaker is Priam. φωριαμῶν is the genitive plural of φωριαμός ‘chest’, a box for storing clothes and valuables, and ἐπιθήματα are the ‘lids’ that are put on them. κάλ’ is καλά ‘fine’, neuter plural. ἀνέῳγεν, from ἀνοίγνυμι, has a pluperfect shape but is simply ‘opened’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δώδεκα μὲν περικαλλέας ἔξελε πέπλους,
δώδεκα δ’ ἁπλοΐδας χλαίνας, τόσσους δὲ τάπητας,
τόσσα δὲ φάρεα λευκά, τόσους δ’ ἐπὶ τοῖσι χιτῶνας.
sentences.tr:
enthen dōdeka men perikalleas exele peplous,
dōdeka d’ haploïdas chlainas, tossous de tapētas,
tossa de pharea leuka, tosous d’ epi toisi chitōnas.
sentences.l:
From there twelve very fair robes he took out,
twelve single cloaks, and as many carpets,
as many white cloaks, and as many tunics besides.
sentences.i: From them he took twelve very fair robes, twelve single cloaks and as many carpets, as many white cloaks, and as many tunics as well.
sentences.n: The list of gifts. πέπλους are ‘robes’, a woman’s garment, and περικαλλέας is ‘very fair’. The second line, 24.230, is the same as Odyssey 24.276, and its English is kept. χλαίνας and φάρεα are different garments but both are ‘cloaks’ in our English, as in the Odyssey; ἁπλοΐδας is ‘single’, of one thickness. τάπητες are ‘carpets’, here rugs or coverings, and λευκά is ‘white’. τόσσους and τόσσα mean ‘as many’.

sentences.t:
χρυσοῦ δὲ στήσας ἔφερεν δέκα πάντα τάλαντα,
ἐκ δὲ δύ’ αἴθωνας τρίποδας, πίσυρας δὲ λέβητας,
sentences.tr:
chrysou de stēsas epheren deka panta talanta,
ek de dy’ aithōnas tripodas, pisyras de lebētas,
sentences.l:
And of gold, having weighed it, he carried ten talents in all,
and out two fire-bright tripods, and four cauldrons,
sentences.i: He weighed out and carried ten talents of gold in all, and brought out two fire-bright tripods and four cauldrons,
sentences.n: στήσας is literally ‘having set (it on the scale)’, so ‘having weighed’; τάλαντα are ‘talents’, a weight of gold. ἔφερεν is ‘was carrying’, and ἐκ in the next line goes with it: ‘out (he carried)’. αἴθων is ‘fire-bright’, of the gleam of bronze, and τρίποδας are tripods, three-legged bronze stands or vessels. πίσυρας is the epic ‘four’, and λέβητας are ‘cauldrons’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ δέπας περικαλλές, ὅ οἱ Θρῇκες πόρον ἄνδρες
ἐξεσίην ἐλθόντι μέγα κτέρας·
sentences.tr:
ek de depas perikalles, ho hoi Thrēikes poron andres
exesiēn elthonti mega kteras·
sentences.l:
and out a very fair cup, which to him Thracian men gave
when he came on an embassy, a great possession:
sentences.i: and a very fair cup, which Thracian men gave him when he came on a mission, a great possession;
sentences.n: δέπας is ‘cup’ and περικαλλές ‘very fair’. ὅ οἱ is ‘which … to him’, and πόρον is the epic aorist ‘they gave’. ἐξεσίην ἐλθόντι is ‘to him as he came on an embassy’, with ἐξεσίη a mission or errand; the Greek does not say what it was about. κτέρας is ‘possession’, and the colon after it prepares the point that Priam did not spare even this.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νυ τοῦ περ
φείσατ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροις ὃ γέρων, περὶ δ’ ἤθελε θυμῷ
λύσασθαι φίλον υἱόν.
sentences.tr:
oude ny tou per
pheisat’ eni megarois ho gerōn, peri d’ ēthele thymōi
lysasthai philon huion.
sentences.l:
nor even of this, then,
did he spare, in the halls, the old man, but exceedingly he wished in heart
to ransom his dear son.
sentences.i: The old man did not spare even this in his halls, so greatly did he wish in his heart to ransom his dear son.
sentences.n: οὐδέ … τοῦ περ is ‘not even of this’, with the genitive of φείδομαι ‘spare’; τοῦ is the Thracian cup. φείσατ’ is the aorist. ὃ γέρων is ‘the old man’, with ὁ as the article. περὶ δ’ ἤθελε is ‘exceedingly he wished’, with περί as an adverb. λύσασθαι is the middle infinitive ‘to ransom’, the word for buying back a captive.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ Τρῶας μὲν ἅπαντας
αἰθούσης ἀπέεργεν ἔπεσσ’ αἰσχροῖσιν ἐνίσσων·
sentences.tr:
ho de Trōas men hapantas
aithousēs apeergen epess’ aischroisin enissōn·
sentences.l:
And he all the Trojans
from the portico was driving off, with shameful words rebuking:
sentences.i: He drove all the Trojans away from the portico, rebuking them with shameful words:
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘and he’, Priam. αἰθούσης is the genitive ‘from the portico’, the roofed porch on the front of a house, with ἀπέεργεν ‘was keeping off, driving away’. The Trojans are the people who have gathered round him. ἐνίσσων is a participle of ἐνίσσω, a by-form of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, and αἰσχροῖσιν ἔπεσσιν ‘shameful words’ names the kind of speech, which follows.

sentences.t:
ἔρρετε λωβητῆρες ἐλεγχέες· οὔ νυ καὶ ὑμῖν
οἴκοι ἔνεστι γόος, ὅτι μ’ ἤλθετε κηδήσοντες;
sentences.tr:
errete lōbētēres elenchees· ou ny kai hymin
oikoi enesti goos, hoti m’ ēlthete kēdēsontes;
sentences.l:
“Be gone, outragers, shameful ones! Is there not, then, even for you
at home lament, that you have come to distress me?
sentences.i: “Be gone, you shameful outragers! Is there not lament at home for you too, that you have come to distress me?
sentences.n: ἔρρετε is an imperative, ‘be gone, away with you’. λωβητῆρες are ‘outragers’, and ἐλεγχέες ‘shameful ones’ is a vocative plural. οὔ νυ expects the answer ‘yes’: they too have griefs of their own. οἴκοι is ‘at home’, ἔνεστι ‘is in’, and γόος ‘lament’. κηδήσοντες is a future participle of κήδω ‘distress’, giving the purpose: ‘to distress me’.

sentences.t:
ἦ ὀνόσασθ’ ὅτι μοι Κρονίδης Ζεὺς ἄλγε’ ἔδωκε
παῖδ’ ὀλέσαι τὸν ἄριστον;
sentences.tr:
ē onosasth’ hoti moi Kronidēs Zeus alge’ edōke
paid’ olesai ton ariston;
sentences.l:
Or do you make light of it that to me Zeus, the son-of-Cronus, gave pains,
the child to lose, the best?
sentences.i: Or do you make light of it that Zeus, the son of Cronus, has given me pains, to lose my best son?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a second question. ὀνόσασθ’ is ὀνόσασθε, the aorist of ὄνομαι ‘make light of’ (LSJ also glosses it ‘find fault with’), with ὅτι ‘that’. Κρονίδης Ζεύς is ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’. ἄλγεα are ‘pains’, and ὀλέσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to lose’, saying what the pains consist of. παῖδα … τὸν ἄριστον is ‘the child, the best’, that is Hector, not named.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ γνώσεσθε καὶ ὔμμες·
ῥηΐτεροι γὰρ μᾶλλον Ἀχαιοῖσιν δὴ ἔσεσθε
κείνου τεθνηῶτος ἐναιρέμεν.
sentences.tr:
atar gnōsesthe kai ymmes·
rhēïteroi gar mallon Achaioisin dē esesthe
keinou tethnēōtos enairemen.
sentences.i: But you too will come to know it: now that he is dead, you will be all the easier for the Achaeans to slay.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘but’, and ὔμμες is the Aeolic form of ὑμεῖς ‘you’. ῥηΐτεροι is the comparative ‘easier’, with Ἀχαιοῖσιν ‘for the Achaeans’ and ἐναιρέμεν ‘to slay’ (epic infinitive, ἐναίρω). κείνου τεθνηῶτος is a genitive absolute: ‘he having died’, the perfect participle of θνῄσκω. μᾶλλον is ‘the more’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
πρὶν ἀλαπαζομένην τε πόλιν κεραϊζομένην τε
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδεῖν βαίην δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω.
sentences.tr:
autar egōge
prin alapazomenēn te polin keraïzomenēn te
ophthalmoisin idein baiēn domon Aïdos eisō.
sentences.l:
But I, for my part,
before the city being laid waste and being ravaged
with my eyes to see, may I go into the house of Hades.”
sentences.i: But for my part, may I go into the house of Hades before I see with my eyes the city laid waste and ravaged.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends this speech. βαίην is an aorist optative of wish, ‘may I go’. πρὶν … ἰδεῖν is ‘before seeing’. The two participles ἀλαπαζομένην and κεραϊζομένην are in the accusative with πόλιν, ‘the city being laid waste and ravaged’. δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω is ‘into the house of Hades’, the underworld as the dwelling of the god.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ σκηπανίῳ δίεπ’ ἀνέρας· οἳ δ’ ἴσαν ἔξω
σπερχομένοιο γέροντος·
sentences.tr:
ē kai skēpaniōi diep’ aneras· hoi d’ isan exō
sperchomenoio gerontos·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and with his staff he drove the men off; and they went out,
the old man hastening:
sentences.i: So he said, and drove the men off with his staff; and they went out, with the old man in haste:
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he said, and’. σκηπανίῳ is a rare word, a dative, ‘with a staff’, a walking-stick, not the royal sceptre. δίεπ’ is an elided διέπε, from a rare verb διέπω; ‘drove off’ is the usual sense given. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἔξω ‘out’. σπερχομένοιο γέροντος is a genitive absolute, ‘the old man being in haste’; σπέρχομαι can mean both hurry and rage.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ υἱάσιν οἷσιν ὁμόκλα
νεικείων Ἕλενόν τε Πάριν τ’ Ἀγάθωνά τε δῖον
Πάμμονά τ’ Ἀντίφονόν τε βοὴν ἀγαθόν τε Πολίτην
Δηΐφοβόν τε καὶ Ἱππόθοον καὶ δῖον Ἀγαυόν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ huiasin hoisin homokla
neikeiōn Helenon te Parin t’ Agathōna te dion
Pammona t’ Antiphonon te boēn agathon te Politēn
Dēïphobon te kai Hippothoon kai dion Agauon·
sentences.l:
and he at his own sons shouted,
reviling Helenus and Paris and Agathon, heavenly,
and Pammon and Antiphonus and Polites, good at the war-cry,
and Deiphobus and Hippothous and heavenly Agauus:
sentences.i: and he shouted at his own sons, reviling Helenus and Paris and heavenly Agathon, and Pammon and Antiphonus and Polites, good at the war-cry, and Deiphobus and Hippothous and heavenly Agauus:
sentences.n: The sons are named, nine of them, as the next line says. ὁμόκλα is ‘shouted at’, with the dative υἱάσιν οἷσιν ‘at his own sons’, and νεικείων ‘reviling’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ marks Agathon and Agauus, βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ marks Polites. Helenus, Paris and Deiphobus are the best known of them from elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: ἐννέα τοῖς ὃ γεραιὸς ὁμοκλήσας ἐκέλευε·
sentences.tr: ennea tois ho geraios homoklēsas ekeleue·
sentences.l: Nine, to these the old man, having shouted at them, ordered:
sentences.i: The old man shouted at those nine and ordered them:
sentences.n: ἐννέα ‘nine’ stands in apposition to τοῖς ‘to them’, the sons just named, and there are nine names in the lines before. ὁμοκλήσας is the aorist participle ‘having shouted at’, the same verb as ὁμόκλα above. ὁ γεραιός is ‘the old man’, and ἐκέλευε is the imperfect ‘was ordering’ with a colon after it, so the order follows.

sentences.t:
σπεύσατέ μοι κακὰ τέκνα κατηφόνες· αἴθ’ ἅμα πάντες
Ἕκτορος ὠφέλετ’ ἀντὶ θοῇς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ πεφάσθαι.
sentences.tr:
speusate moi kaka tekna katēphones· aith’ hama pantes
Hektoros ōphelet’ anti thoēis epi nēusi pephasthai.
sentences.l:
“Hurry, for me, base children, shames; would that all together
you had been slain in Hector’s place by the swift ships.
sentences.i: “Hurry, you base children, you shames! If only all of you together had been killed beside the swift ships in Hector’s place.
sentences.n: σπεύσατε is an aorist imperative ‘hurry’, and μοι ‘for me’ shows his interest in the speed. κακὰ τέκνα is ‘base children’, and κατηφόνες is ‘shames’, people who bring shame, said to come from κατηφής ‘downcast’; the speech goes on in the next units. αἴθ’ … ὠφέλετ’ … πεφάσθαι is a wish for the past, ‘would that you had been killed’, with πεφάσθαι the perfect passive infinitive of φένω ‘slay’. ἀντὶ Ἕκτορος is ‘in Hector’s place’, and θοῇς is the epic dative ‘swift’.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι ἐγὼ πανάποτμος, ἐπεὶ τέκον υἷας ἀρίστους
Τροίῃ ἐν εὐρείῃ, τῶν δ’ οὔ τινά φημι λελεῖφθαι,
sentences.tr:
ō moi egō panapotmos, epei tekon huias aristous
Troiēi en eureiēi, tōn d’ ou tina phēmi leleiphthai,
sentences.l:
Oh me, I utterly ill-fated, since I begot the best sons
in wide Troy, and of them not one, I say, is left,
sentences.i: Oh me, utterly ill-fated that I am: I fathered the best of sons in wide Troy, and I say that none of them is left,
sentences.n: πανάποτμος is ‘utterly ill-fated’, made from πᾶν ‘all’ and ἄποτμος ‘ill-fated’. ἐπεὶ τέκον, ‘since I begot’, gives the reason; τέκον is the aorist of τίκτω, said of a father here. υἷας is the epic accusative of υἱός. τῶν δ’ οὔ τινά φημι λελεῖφθαι is ‘and of them I say that not one is left’, with the perfect passive infinitive of λείπω; the three names follow in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Μήστορά τ’ ἀντίθεον καὶ Τρωΐλον ἱππιοχάρμην
Ἕκτορά θ’, ὃς θεὸς ἔσκε μετ’ ἀνδράσιν, οὐδὲ ἐῴκει
ἀνδρός γε θνητοῦ πάϊς ἔμμεναι ἀλλὰ θεοῖο.
sentences.tr:
Mēstora t’ antitheon kai Trōïlon hippiocharmēn
Hektora th’, hos theos eske met’ andrasin, oude eōikei
andros ge thnētou païs emmenai alla theoio.
sentences.l:
Mestor, godlike, and Troilus, the chariot-fighter,
and Hector, who was a god among men, and was not like
to be a mortal man’s son, but a god’s.
sentences.i: Mestor, godlike, and Troilus, the chariot-fighter, and Hector, who was a god among men and did not seem to be the son of a mortal man, but of a god.
sentences.n: The three names pick out sons from ‘the best sons’ of 24.255, all now dead. ἀντίθεος is ‘godlike’, and ἱππιοχάρμης is ‘chariot-fighter’, from ἵππος ‘horse’ and χάρμη ‘battle’. ἔσκε is an old iterative form of ‘was’. οὐδὲ ἐῴκει is ‘and he did not seem’, from ἔοικα. πάϊς is ‘son’, ἔμμεναι the epic infinitive ‘to be’, and θνητοῦ ‘mortal’. Hector is the only one for whom he says more.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ἀπώλεσ’ Ἄρης, τὰ δ’ ἐλέγχεα πάντα λέλειπται
ψεῦσταί τ’ ὀρχησταί τε χοροιτυπίῃσιν ἄριστοι
ἀρνῶν ἠδ’ ἐρίφων ἐπιδήμιοι ἁρπακτῆρες.
sentences.tr:
tous men apōles’ Arēs, ta d’ elenchea panta leleiptai
pseustai t’ orchēstai te choroitypiēisin aristoi
arnōn ēd’ eriphōn epidēmioi harpaktēres.
sentences.l:
Those Ares destroyed, but the disgraces are all left,
liars and dancers, the best in dance-stamping,
plunderers at home of lambs and kids.
sentences.i: Ares destroyed those, but all the disgraces are left, liars and dancers, the best at stamping out the dance, plunderers of lambs and kids among their own people.
sentences.n: Ἄρης is Ares as the war-god and war itself. τὰ ἐλέγχεα are ‘the disgraces’, here persons, and the next two lines list them. ψεῦσται ‘liars’, ὀρχησταί ‘dancers’; χοροιτυπίῃσιν is the dative plural ‘in dance-stamping’, the beating of feet in a chorus. ἐπιδήμιοι is ‘among the people, at home’, and ἁρπακτῆρες are ‘plunderers’. λέλειπται is the perfect passive ‘have been left’.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν δή μοι ἄμαξαν ἐφοπλίσσαιτε τάχιστα,
ταῦτά τε πάντ’ ἐπιθεῖτε, ἵνα πρήσσωμεν ὁδοῖο;
sentences.tr:
ouk an dē moi amaxan ephoplissaite tachista,
tauta te pant’ epitheite, hina prēssōmen hodoio;
sentences.l:
Will you not, then, make ready a wagon for me as quickly as possible,
and put on it all these things, so that we may accomplish the journey?”
sentences.i: Will you not make a wagon ready for me as quickly as you can, and put all these things on it, so that we may complete the journey?”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends this speech. οὐκ ἂν … ἐφοπλίσσαιτε is an optative with ἄν used as a sharp order in the form of a question: ‘won’t you make ready?’. ἄμαξαν is ‘wagon’, and τάχιστα the superlative ‘as quickly as possible’. ἐπιθεῖτε is the aorist optative of ἐπιτίθημι, ‘put on’. πρήσσωμεν is a subjunctive of πράσσω ‘accomplish’, with ὁδοῖο ‘the journey’ as its genitive object.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πατρὸς ὑποδείσαντες ὁμοκλὴν
ἐκ μὲν ἄμαξαν ἄειραν ἐΰτροχον ἡμιονείην
καλὴν πρωτοπαγέα, πείρινθα δὲ δῆσαν ἐπ’ αὐτῆς,
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara patros hypodeisantes homoklēn
ek men amaxan aeiran eÿtrochon hēmioneiēn
kalēn prōtopagea, peirintha de dēsan ep’ autēs,
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they, fearing their father’s shouted rebuke,
lifted out a wagon, well-rolling, mule-drawn,
fine, newly built, and a basket they bound upon it,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they, afraid of their father’s shouted rebuke, lifted out a fine, newly built, well-rolling, mule-drawn wagon, and bound a basket on it,
sentences.n: The sons act at once. ὑποδείσαντες is ‘having feared’, and ὁμοκλήν is ‘shouted rebuke’. ἐκ … ἄειραν, split apart, is ‘lifted out’. ἐΰτροχον ἡμιονείην is the usual ‘well-rolling, mule-drawn’. πρωτοπαγέα, from πρῶτος ‘first’ and πήγνυμι ‘fix’, is read as ‘newly made’. πείρινθα is a ‘basket’, a body fixed on the wagon, and its exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἀπὸ πασσαλόφι ζυγὸν ᾕρεον ἡμιόνειον
πύξινον ὀμφαλόεν εὖ οἰήκεσσιν ἀρηρός·
sentences.tr:
kad d’ apo passalophi zygon hēireon hēmioneion
pyxinon omphaloen eu oiēkessin arēros·
sentences.l:
and down from the peg they took the yoke, a mule-yoke,
of boxwood, bossed, well fitted with rings;
sentences.i: and from the peg they took down the mule yoke, of boxwood, bossed, well fitted with rings;
sentences.n: κὰδ … ᾕρεον is ‘took down’ (κάδ is κατά). πασσαλόφι is ‘from the peg’, with the old ending -φι. ζυγὸν ἡμιόνειον is ‘a mule yoke’, πύξινον ‘of boxwood’, and ὀμφαλόεν ‘bossed’, having a knob. οἰήκεσσιν is usually taken as the rings or loops on the yoke through which the reins passed; ἀρηρός is ‘fitted’, so ‘well fitted with them’. The raised stop after it opens the next piece.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἔφερον ζυγόδεσμον ἅμα ζυγῷ ἐννεάπηχυ.
sentences.tr: ek d’ epheron zygodesmon hama zygōi enneapēchy.
sentences.l: and out they carried the yoke-band along with the yoke, nine cubits long.
sentences.i: and they brought out the yoke-band with the yoke, nine cubits long.
sentences.n: ζυγόδεσμον is ‘yoke-band’, the strap that binds the yoke to the pole, and ἅμα ζυγῷ is ‘along with the yoke’. ἐννεάπηχυ is ‘nine-cubit’, a πῆχυς being a forearm’s length (a cubit), whose measure was not exactly fixed. ἐκ … ἔφερον is the tmesis ‘carried out’, the same ‘out’ as at 266.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν εὖ κατέθηκαν ἐϋξέστῳ ἐπὶ ῥυμῷ
πέζῃ ἔπι πρώτῃ, ἐπὶ δὲ κρίκον ἕστορι βάλλον,
sentences.tr:
kai to men eu katethēkan eÿxestōi epi rhymōi
pezēi epi prōtēi, epi de krikon hestori ballon,
sentences.l:
and this they set well on the well-polished pole
at the foremost end, and on the pin they threw the ring,
sentences.i: They set the yoke well on the well-polished pole, at its foremost end, and threw the ring on the pin,
sentences.n: The harness details are technical, and the translation is tentative. τὸ μέν is ‘this’, most likely the yoke (the yoke-band is the other candidate). ῥυμῷ is the ‘pole’ and πέζῃ πρώτῃ ‘at its first foot, the front end’. κρίκον is ‘ring’ and ἕστορι ‘on the pin’, a peg on the pole that the ring slides over. βάλλον is the imperfect ‘were throwing, put’. ἐϋξέστῳ is ‘well-polished’.

sentences.t:
τρὶς δ’ ἑκάτερθεν ἔδησαν ἐπ’ ὀμφαλόν, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ἑξείης κατέδησαν, ὑπὸ γλωχῖνα δ’ ἔκαμψαν.
sentences.tr:
tris d’ hekaterthen edēsan ep’ omphalon, autar epeita
hexeiēs katedēsan, hypo glōchina d’ ekampsan.
sentences.l:
and three times on each side they bound it to the boss, and then
in order they tied it down, and under the point they bent it.
sentences.i: Three times on each side they lashed it to the boss, and then bound it down in order, and bent it under the point.
sentences.n: ἐπ’ ὀμφαλόν is ‘to the boss’, a knob on the yoke, which was called ὀμφαλόεν ‘bossed’ at 24.269. The strap (the yoke-band) is the unstated object. ἑξείης is ‘in order’, and κατέδησαν ‘bound down’. γλωχῖνα is the accusative of γλωχίς, a projecting point or tip; ἔκαμψαν ‘they bent’ the loose end under it. As with the lines before, the exact fastening is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἐκ θαλάμου δὲ φέροντες ἐϋξέστης ἐπ’ ἀπήνης
νήεον Ἑκτορέης κεφαλῆς ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα,
sentences.tr:
ek thalamou de pherontes eÿxestēs ep’ apēnēs
nēeon Hektoreēs kephalēs apereisi’ apoina,
sentences.l:
and bringing from the chamber onto the well-polished wagon
they heaped up the unstinted ransom for Hector’s head,
sentences.i: They brought the unstinted ransom for Hector’s head out of the chamber and loaded it onto the well-polished wagon,
sentences.n: θαλάμου is ‘from the chamber’, the storeroom of the previous scene. ἀπήνη is another word for the wagon, and both words are ‘wagon’ in our English. νήεον is the imperfect of νηέω ‘heap up, load’. Ἑκτορέης is the adjective ‘of Hector’, so Ἑκτορέης κεφαλῆς is ‘for Hector’s head’, with head standing for the man. ἄποινα is ‘ransom’ and ἀπερείσι’ ‘unstinted’.

sentences.t:
ζεῦξαν δ’ ἡμιόνους κρατερώνυχας ἐντεσιεργούς,
τούς ῥά ποτε Πριάμῳ Μυσοὶ δόσαν ἀγλαὰ δῶρα.
sentences.tr:
zeuxan d’ hēmionous kraterōnychas entesiergous,
tous rha pote Priamōi Mysoi dosan aglaa dōra.
sentences.l:
and they yoked the mules, strong-hooved, harness-workers,
which once the Mysians gave to Priam, splendid gifts.
sentences.i: They yoked the strong-hooved mules that work in harness, which the Mysians had once given Priam, splendid gifts.
sentences.n: ζεῦξαν is the aorist ‘yoked’, and ἡμιόνους ‘mules’. κρατερώνυχας is ‘strong-hooved’, from κρατερός ‘strong’ and ὄνυξ ‘nail, hoof’. ἐντεσιεργούς, ‘working in the harness’, is probably formed on ἔντεα ‘gear’ and ἔργον ‘work’. The Mysians are a people of Asia Minor. τούς is the relative ‘which’, ῥά ποτε ‘once’, δόσαν the epic ‘gave’, and ἀγλαὰ δῶρα ‘splendid gifts’.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δὲ Πριάμῳ ὕπαγον ζυγόν, οὓς ὃ γεραιὸς
αὐτὸς ἔχων ἀτίταλλεν ἐϋξέστῃ ἐπὶ φάτνῃ.
sentences.tr:
hippous de Priamōi hypagon zygon, hous ho geraios
autos echōn atitallen eÿxestēi epi phatnēi.
sentences.l:
And for Priam they led horses under the yoke, which the old man
himself kept and reared at the well-polished manger.
sentences.i: And for Priam they led horses under the yoke, which the old man himself kept and reared at the well-polished manger.
sentences.n: ὕπαγον ζυγόν is ‘led under the yoke’; the mules just yoked are for the wagon, and these horses are separate. οὓς … ἔχων is ‘which, keeping’, and ἀτίταλλεν is ‘reared’, the care of an animal one has brought up. αὐτός is ‘himself’. φάτνῃ is ‘manger’ and ἐϋξέστῃ ‘well-polished’.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ζευγνύσθην ἐν δώμασιν ὑψηλοῖσι
κῆρυξ καὶ Πρίαμος πυκινὰ φρεσὶ μήδε’ ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
tō men zeugnysthēn en dōmasin hypsēloisi
kēryx kai Priamos pykina phresi mēde’ echontes·
sentences.l:
Those two were yoking in the high house,
the herald and Priam, solid counsels having in their wits:
sentences.i: The two of them, the herald and Priam, were yoking in the high house, each with solid counsels in his wits:
sentences.n: τὼ μέν is a dual, ‘those two’, and so is ζευγνύσθην. The object of the yoking is not named; the lines just before have the sons yoking mules and leading horses up. κῆρυξ is ‘herald’, the older man Zeus spoke of at 24.149, who will drive. πυκινὰ μήδεα is ‘solid counsels’, and the participle ἔχοντες is plural although the verb is dual.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δέ σφ’ ἦλθ’ Ἑκάβη τετιηότι θυμῷ
οἶνον ἔχουσ’ ἐν χειρὶ μελίφρονα δεξιτερῆφι
χρυσέῳ ἐν δέπαϊ, ὄφρα λείψαντε κιοίτην·
sentences.tr:
anchimolon de sph’ ēlth’ Hekabē tetiēoti thymōi
oinon echous’ en cheiri meliphrona dexiterēphi
chryseōi en depaï, ophra leipsante kioitēn·
sentences.l:
And close by them came Hecuba, with grieved heart,
holding honey-hearted wine in her right hand
in a golden cup, so that having poured a libation the two might set out:
sentences.i: Close beside them came Hecuba, grieved at heart, holding heart-sweetening wine in her right hand in a golden cup, so that the two of them might pour a libation and set out:
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is ‘close by’, σφ’ is σφε ‘them (two)’, and τετιηότι θυμῷ ‘with grieved heart’. μελίφρονα, from μέλι ‘honey’ and φρήν ‘heart, wits’, is traditionally ‘heart-sweetening’ and its sense is uncertain. δεξιτερῆφι is ‘in the right hand’, with the old ending -φι. λείψαντε is a dual aorist participle of λείβω ‘pour a libation’, and κιοίτην a dual optative of κίω ‘go’.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἵππων προπάροιθεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr: stē d’ hippōn proparoithen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l: and she stood in front of the horses, and spoke a word and called him by name:
sentences.i: and she stood in front of the horses and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist ‘stood’, and ἵππων προπάροιθεν is ‘in front of the horses’, so she blocks the way. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is the poet’s ordinary line for introducing a speech: ἔφατ’ is ‘spoke’, and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε, split apart, is ‘named out, called by name’. The one addressed is Priam, who is not named.

sentences.t:
τῆ σπεῖσον Διὶ πατρί, καὶ εὔχεο οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι
ἂψ ἐκ δυσμενέων ἀνδρῶν, ἐπεὶ ἂρ σέ γε θυμὸς
ὀτρύνει ἐπὶ νῆας ἐμεῖο μὲν οὐκ ἐθελούσης.
sentences.tr:
tē speison Dii patri, kai eucheo oikad’ hikesthai
aps ek dysmeneōn andrōn, epei ar se ge thymos
otrynei epi nēas emeio men ouk ethelousēs.
sentences.l:
“Here, pour a libation to father Zeus, and pray to come home
again from the ill-disposed men, since your heart
urges you to the ships, though I do not wish it.
sentences.i: “Here, pour a libation to father Zeus, and pray to come home again from among the ill-disposed men, since your heart urges you to the ships, though I do not wish it.
sentences.n: τῆ is an old word used when handing over something: ‘here, take this’, with the cup. σπεῖσον and εὔχεο are imperatives, ‘pour a libation’ and ‘pray’. οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι is ‘to arrive home’, and ἂψ ‘back’. δυσμενέων is ‘ill-disposed’. ὀτρύνει is ‘urges’, and ἐμεῖο … οὐκ ἐθελούσης is a genitive absolute, ‘I not wishing’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εὔχεο σύ γ’ ἔπειτα κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίωνι
Ἰδαίῳ, ὅς τε Τροίην κατὰ πᾶσαν ὁρᾶται,
sentences.tr:
all’ eucheo sy g’ epeita kelainepheï Kroniōni
Idaiōi, hos te Troiēn kata pasan horatai,
sentences.l:
But pray you then to the dark-clouded son of Cronus,
the Idaean, who over all Troy looks about,
sentences.i: But then pray to the son of Cronus of the dark clouds, the Idaean, who looks over all Troy,
sentences.n: σύ γ’ ἔπειτα is ‘you, then’, after the libation. κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίωνι is ‘the dark-clouded son of Cronus’, Zeus. Ἰδαίῳ is ‘of Ida’, the mountain above Troy where Zeus has his seat. ὁρᾶται is a middle or passive form of ὁράω. It is taken as a middle with active sense, ‘looks about over’ (Zeus surveys all Troy from Ida); read as a passive it would mean ‘is seen’, which suits the sentence less well.

sentences.t:
αἴτει δ’ οἰωνὸν ταχὺν ἄγγελον, ὅς τέ οἱ αὐτῷ
φίλτατος οἰωνῶν, καί εὑ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον,
sentences.tr:
aitei d’ oiōnon tachyn angelon, hos te hoi autōi
philtatos oiōnōn, kai heu kratos esti megiston,
sentences.l:
and ask for a bird of omen, a swift messenger, which to him himself
is dearest of birds, and its strength is greatest,
sentences.i: and ask for a swift bird of omen as a messenger, the one that is dearest to him of all birds and whose strength is greatest,
sentences.n: αἴτει is ‘ask for’. οἰωνός is a bird seen as an omen, here a messenger from Zeus. ταχύν is ‘swift’, ἄγγελον ‘messenger’. οἱ αὐτῷ is ‘to him himself’, Zeus. φίλτατος is ‘dearest’. καί εὑ κράτος … μέγιστον is ‘and of it the strength is greatest’, with εὑ a form of ‘of it’. The bird is not named; its description fits the eagle.

sentences.t:
δεξιόν, ὄφρά μιν αὐτὸς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσι νοήσας
τῷ πίσυνος ἐπὶ νῆας ἴῃς Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων.
sentences.tr:
dexion, ophra min autos en ophthalmoisi noēsas
tōi pisynos epi nēas iēis Danaōn tachypōlōn.
sentences.l:
on the right, so that, seeing it yourself with your eyes,
trusting in it you may go to the ships of the swift-colted Danaans.
sentences.i: a bird on the right, so that you may see it for yourself with your own eyes and, trusting in it, go to the ships of the Danaans with their swift colts.
sentences.n: δεξιόν ‘on the right’ agrees with οἰωνόν. The right was the lucky side for a sign. νοήσας is ‘perceiving’, αὐτός ‘yourself’, and ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσι ‘in your eyes’. πίσυνος is ‘trusting in’, with the dative τῷ ‘in it’. ἴῃς is the subjunctive of εἶμι ‘you may go’. Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων is ‘the Danaans with their swift colts’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τοι οὐ δώσει ἑὸν ἄγγελον εὐρύοπα Ζεύς,
οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγέ σ’ ἔπειτα ἐποτρύνουσα κελοίμην
νῆας ἐπ’ Ἀργείων ἰέναι μάλα περ μεμαῶτα.
sentences.tr:
ei de toi ou dōsei heon angelon euryopa Zeus,
ouk an egōge s’ epeita epotrynousa keloimēn
nēas ep’ Argeiōn ienai mala per memaōta.
sentences.l:
But if far-thundering Zeus will not give you his own messenger,
then I for my part would not urge you, urging you on,
to go to the ships of the Argives, very eager though you are.”
sentences.i: But if Zeus who thunders from afar will not give you his own messenger, then I for my part would not urge you, pressing you on, to go to the ships of the Argives, eager as you are.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Hecuba’s speech. εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is ‘far-thundering Zeus’, an old epithet whose second part is disputed. ἑὸν ἄγγελον is ‘his own messenger’, the omen bird. οὐκ ἂν … κελοίμην is an optative with ἄν, ‘I would not urge’, and ἐποτρύνουσα ‘urging on’. μάλα περ μεμαῶτα is ‘very eager though you are’, with μεμαῶτα an accusative agreeing with σέ. Ἀργείων is the third of the army’s names to appear in this part, after Ἀχαιῶν and Δαναῶν.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē Priamos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: In answer Priam, godlike in form, said to her:
sentences.n: ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, and προσέφη ‘addressed’; together they are the regular formula for a reply. τὴν is ‘her’, Hecuba. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’, as at 24.217, and is Priam’s epithet whenever he speaks to her in this part.

sentences.t: ὦ γύναι οὐ μέν τοι τόδ’ ἐφιεμένῃ ἀπιθήσω.
sentences.tr: ō gynai ou men toi tod’ ephiemenēi apithēsō.
sentences.l: “Woman, I will not disobey you in this, as you urge it.
sentences.i: “Woman, I will not disobey you in this, as you urge it.
sentences.n: ὦ γύναι is ‘woman’, a respectful form of address to a wife. οὐ μέν τοι stresses the denial: ‘surely not’. τόδ’ ἐφιεμένῃ is a dative participle, ‘you urging this’, with τοι (σοι) ‘to you’. ἀπιθήσω is the future of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’. He is yielding, after refusing at 24.218–219.

sentences.t: ἐσθλὸν γὰρ Διὶ χεῖρας ἀνασχέμεν αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ.
sentences.tr: esthlon gar Dii cheiras anaschemen ai k’ eleēsēi.
sentences.l: For it is good to raise the hands to Zeus, in case he takes pity.”
sentences.i: For it is good to raise one’s hands to Zeus, in case he takes pity.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Priam’s speech; the part ends here, at the paragraph’s close. ἐσθλόν is ‘good’, and the infinitive χεῖρας ἀνασχέμεν ‘to raise the hands’ is its subject. αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ is ‘in case he takes pity’, with a subjunctive. Priam does not say that Zeus will pity him, only that to ask is right.
